prompt: Why do elements in the same group of the periodic table tend to have similar chemical properties?

choices.text: They have the same configuration of s and p valence electrons
They have the same number of electron shells
choices.why: Elements in the same row share a shell number. Group members share the same s and p valence electron configuration.

choices.text: They have the same atomic mass
choices.why: Atomic mass rises steeply down a group. The shared valence electron configuration is what makes group members alike.

choices.text: They have the same atomic radius
choices.why: Radius increases down a group. Group members are alike because their valence configurations match.

explanation: The number of valence electrons and the types of orbitals they occupy are determined by an element's group, so elements in a group have the same configuration of s and p valence electrons. This is one reason they have similar chemical properties, and why it is convenient to discuss the elements by group.

prompt: Valence orbital energy decreases from left to right across a row. What is the major factor driving this decrease?

choices.text: The increase in effective nuclear charge, Z*, which strengthens the electron–nucleus attraction
The increase in the principal quantum number
choices.why: The principal quantum number stays the same across a row; it increases down a group.

choices.text: The decreasing size of the valence orbitals, which outweighs any change in charge
choices.why: Shrinking size does reinforce the effect, but the section says it matters less than the rising charge: Z* increases by about 2/3 of a charge unit from group to group while size falls only gradually.

choices.text: The decreasing number of valence electrons
choices.why: The number of valence electrons increases across a row.

explanation: Across a row the effective nuclear charge rises by about 2/3 of a charge unit per group, increasing the electron–nucleus attraction and lowering the valence orbital energy. The accompanying decrease in orbital size reinforces this, but is less important than the increasing charge.

prompt: According to the section, why are metals malleable and ductile?

choices.text: Their delocalized bonding lets the lattice deform by dislocation movement (slip) without significantly disrupting the bonding
Their atoms are held together by strong, directional pairwise covalent bonds
choices.why: Directional covalent bonds would have to break on deformation, which is why covalent solids are brittle. Metals are held together by delocalized bonding.

choices.text: They have a large band gap between filled and empty bands
choices.why: A large band gap is typical of nonmetal network solids. Metals have an incompletely filled valence band.

choices.text: Their solids are held together only by weak intermolecular forces
choices.why: That describes molecular solids, which are brittle or soft. Metals are held together by delocalized metallic bonding.

explanation: Metals form solids held together by delocalized bonding. Their lattices can be deformed by dislocation movement (slip) without significantly disrupting that bonding, so they can be hammered into sheets and pulled into wires. Their incompletely filled, delocalized valence band also makes them good conductors of heat and electricity.

prompt: Nonmetals usually have low electrical conductivity, yet graphite is an outstanding electrical conductor. Why?

choices.text: Its π valence band and π* conduction band overlap, leaving no band gap
Graphite is a metal
choices.why: Carbon is a nonmetal. Graphite conducts because of its band structure, not because it is metallic.

choices.text: Its strong σ bonds give a large band gap
choices.why: A large band gap would make it an insulator. Graphite conducts because its π bands overlap with no gap.

choices.text: Electrons move between separate molecules by collisions
choices.why: Transfer by collisions is very slow and is why molecular solids conduct poorly. Graphite is a network solid with overlapping π bands.

explanation: Low conductivity is only a tendency for nonmetals. Network covalent solids held together by weaker covalent bonds or π bonds sometimes have small or nonexistent band gaps. Graphite's π valence band and π* conduction band overlap, so there is no band gap and it conducts well.

prompt: Why does hydrogen have an ambiguous position in the periodic table?

choices.text: It has a single valence electron that it readily loses, like the alkali metals, but it is also one electron short of a filled shell and readily forms hydrides, like the halogens
Its 1s orbital is full, compact, and low in energy, so it forms no compounds
choices.why: That describes helium, which has a filled 1s orbital and no known compounds. Hydrogen's half-filled 1s orbital makes it reactive.

choices.text: Its electronegativity is identical to that of lithium
choices.why: Hydrogen's electronegativity is much greater than lithium's, which is part of why its placement above the alkali metals is uneasy.

choices.text: It has valence electrons in both s and p orbitals
choices.why: Hydrogen's valence shell is only a 1s orbital.

explanation: Hydrogen's valence shell is only the 1s orbital, which holds one electron. It readily loses that electron, especially in water, so it is usually placed at the head of the alkali metals. But it is also just one electron short of a filled shell and readily forms hydrides, so it could be placed above the halogens. Some tables place H above the table to stress this versatility.

prompt: Nitrogen and oxygen exist as diatomic gases held together by multiple bonds, but phosphorus and sulfur form singly bonded clusters and chains. What explains this difference?

choices.text: Row 2 elements form strong π bonds because their compact orbitals and short bonds give significant π overlap; the large, diffuse orbitals of heavier elements give weak π bonds
Phosphorus and sulfur have fewer valence electrons than nitrogen and oxygen
choices.why: P and S have the same number of valence electrons as N and O, since they are in the same groups.

choices.text: Row 3 elements cannot form σ bonds
choices.why: Row 3 elements form σ bonds readily; their clusters and chains are held together by single σ bonds. It is their π bonds that are weak.

choices.text: Heavier elements' orbitals are more compact, so they overlap too strongly
choices.why: Orbitals get larger and more diffuse down a group. Less of a diffuse orbital contributes to π overlap, so π bonds are weak.

explanation: Under the uniqueness principle, only the second row elements form strong π bonds: the fraction of electron density involved in π overlap is significant for their compact orbitals and short bonds. For row 3 and heavier elements, relatively little of the large, diffuse orbitals contributes to π overlap, so it is almost always more favorable to form multiple single bonds or engage in cluster bonding.

prompt: Why do row 3 and heavier main group elements form trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral structures more readily than row 2 elements do?

choices.text: Their larger size reduces the steric strain of adding multiple ligands about the central atom
Row 2 elements have more valence electrons than row 3 elements
choices.why: Group members have the same number of valence electrons. The difference is size: row 2 atoms are too small to accommodate more than about four ligands easily.

choices.text: Row 2 elements form only ionic compounds
choices.why: Row 2 elements like C, N, and O form many covalent compounds; they just don't readily exceed a coordination number of four.

choices.text: Row 3 elements cannot form π bonds at all
choices.why: Weak π bonding is a separate difference. High coordination numbers come from the larger size of the heavier atoms.

explanation: When second row elements serve as a central atom, they do not readily exhibit coordination numbers higher than four. The larger size of row 3 and heavier elements reduces the steric strain of adding multiple ligands, making high coordination number structures easier to form.

prompt: SiH4 reacts with ethanol to give Si(OEt)4 and H2, while CH4 does not react. What is the more important, thermodynamic reason for this difference?

choices.text: Silicon is less electronegative than hydrogen, so the Si–H bond is polarized in a way that favors nucleophilic attack at Si and elimination of H2
Silicon is more electronegative than hydrogen, making the Si–H hydrogens acidic
choices.why: It's the reverse: silicon's electronegativity is lower than hydrogen's, so the Si–H hydrogen carries a partial negative charge.

choices.text: The C–H bond is polarized with hydrogen negative, so it repels ethanol
choices.why: Carbon is more electronegative than hydrogen, so in C–H bonds the hydrogen is the partially positive end.

choices.text: Larger Si can form a trigonal bipyramidal intermediate
choices.why: That is the kinetic factor, which lets the reaction happen quickly. The section calls bond polarity the second and much more important factor.

explanation: There is a kinetic factor (larger Si can add a ligand to form a relatively stable trigonal bipyramidal intermediate), but the much more important factor is thermodynamic. Carbon is more electronegative than H, so C–H bonds are polarized in a way that disfavors reaction with alcohols. Silicon is less electronegative than H, so the polarization of Si–H bonds favors nucleophilic attack of the ethanol O at Si and elimination of the Si–H and O–H hydrogens as H2.

prompt: What observation is the Pauling electronegativity scale based on?

choices.text: Polar bonds are generally stronger than the average of their homopolar counterparts
Electronegativity equals the average of the ionization energy and electron affinity
choices.why: That is the Mulliken definition. Pauling's scale is based on the excess strength of polar bonds.

choices.text: Electronegativity is the electrostatic force on a bonding electron from the effective nuclear charge
choices.why: That is the Allred–Rochow approach. Pauling used bond energies.

choices.text: Polar bonds are always weaker than homopolar bonds
choices.why: The opposite: polar bonds tend to be stronger than the average of the corresponding homopolar bonds, and that excess measures the electronegativity difference.

explanation: The Pauling scale uses the "excess bond strength" of a polar bond over the average of its homopolar counterparts as an empirical measure of the electronegativity difference. For example, the average of the H–H and F–F bond energies, 295.5 kJ/mol, is only 52% of the H–F bond energy of 567 kJ/mol. Only differences come from this, so Pauling set F, the most electronegative element, at 4.00 (since adjusted to 3.98).

prompt: In the Pauling model, the "excess bond strength" of a polar A–B bond is how much stronger it is than the average of the A–A and B–B bond energies. If A–A = 432 kJ/mol, B–B = 240 kJ/mol, and A–B = 428 kJ/mol, what is the excess bond strength, in kJ/mol?
explanation: The average of the homopolar bonds is (432 + 240)/2 = 336 kJ/mol. The excess bond strength is 428 − 336 = 92 kJ/mol. The larger the bond polarity, the larger this excess, which is why Pauling used it to measure electronegativity differences.

prompt: Electronegativity usually decreases down a group, but Ga is more electronegative than Al. Why?

choices.text: Filling the d block raises the effective nuclear charge felt by the post-transition elements (a d-block contraction)
Ga has fewer electron shells than Al
choices.why: Ga is below Al, so it has more shells. Its electronegativity is raised by the poorly shielding d electrons added before it.

choices.text: Ga is a nonmetal and Al is a metal
choices.why: Both are metals. The anomaly comes from the increased effective nuclear charge after the d block fills.

choices.text: Electronegativity always increases down group 13
choices.why: The increase happens only between rows 3 and 4 (Al to Ga, and similarly Si to Ge); it is an anomaly caused by d-block filling.

explanation: The post-transition metals have anomalously high electronegativities because of the increasing effective nuclear charge associated with filling the d block, a sort of d-block contraction for electronegativity. For Al & Ga and Si & Ge this reverses the usual trend, so electronegativity increases from row 3 to row 4.

prompt: Which observation illustrates the diagonal relationship between lithium and magnesium?

choices.text: Lithium is the only alkali metal to form a stable nitride (Li3N) and oxide (Li2O), as magnesium forms Mg3N2 and MgO
Lithium forms a superoxide when burned, like magnesium
choices.why: Superoxides and peroxides are formed by the larger alkali metals. Lithium, like Mg, forms the simple oxide.

choices.text: Lithium and magnesium both form insoluble polymeric carbanion reagents
choices.why: Insoluble polymeric carbanion reagents are typical of the larger alkali metals. Alkyllithiums, like Grignard reagents, are THF-soluble.

choices.text: Lithium and magnesium are in the same group
choices.why: Li is in group 1 and Mg in group 2. A diagonal relationship links an element to the one just right of and below it.

explanation: Lithium acts like Mg in being the only alkali metal to form a stable nitride (Li3N), oxide (Li2O), and THF-soluble alkyl carbanion salts (RLi, compare Grignard reagents RMgX). The larger alkali metals form insoluble polymeric carbanion reagents, superoxides or peroxides rather than oxides, and extremely unstable nitrides.

prompt: Why do diagonally related elements, such as Be and Al or B and Si, sometimes have similar properties?

choices.text: The increase in electronegativity across a row is offset by the decrease down a group, and atomic size changes compensate in the same way
Diagonal elements have the same number of valence electrons
choices.why: Diagonal partners are in neighboring groups, so their valence electron counts differ. Their similarity comes from compensating trends.

choices.text: Diagonal elements have identical atomic masses
choices.why: Their masses differ. The similarity comes from compensating trends in electronegativity and size.

choices.text: Diagonal elements are always both metalloids
choices.why: Li & Mg and Be & Al are metals. What they share is similar electronegativity and size.

explanation: Electronegativity increases across a row and decreases down a group, so moving one step right and one step down can leave it nearly unchanged. Atomic size also decreases across a row and increases down a group, so some similarities reflect size effects as well. Examples include Li & Mg, Be & Al (both form amphoteric oxides and hydroxides), and B & Si (both semiconductors with polymeric acidic oxides).

prompt: Al(OH)3 + 3H^+ → Al^3+ + 3H2O and Al(OH)3 + OH^− → Al(OH)4^−. What do these reactions show about aluminum hydroxide?

choices.text: It is amphoteric: it reacts as a base with acid and as a Lewis acid with hydroxide
It is only basic
choices.why: The second reaction shows it accepting OH^− as a Lewis acid, so it isn't only basic.

choices.text: It is only acidic, like the oxides of carbon
choices.why: The first reaction shows it neutralizing H^+ as a base.

choices.text: It is a redox reaction in which Al is oxidized
choices.why: Al stays +3 throughout. These are acid–base reactions.

explanation: The diagonally related elements Be and Al both form amphoteric oxides and hydroxides. Al(OH)3 acts as a base toward H^+ and as a Lewis acid toward OH^−, forming the aluminate ion Al(OH)4^−. Be(OH)2 behaves the same way, giving Be^2+ or Be(OH)4^2−.

prompt: The Mulliken electronegativity is approximated as the average of an atom's ionization energy and electron affinity, both in eV. What is the Mulliken electronegativity, in eV, of an atom with IE = 13.0 eV and EA = 3.6 eV?
explanation: χ ≈ (IE + EA)/2 = (13.0 eV + 3.6 eV)/2 = 8.3 eV. Because IE ≈ −E(HOAO) and EA ≈ −E(LUAO), this is also roughly the negative of the average of the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied orbital energies.

prompt: HClO has pKa 7.40 and HClO2 has pKa 1.94. What explains the stronger acidity of HClO2?

choices.text: Cl is in a higher oxidation state (+3 vs +1), which raises its Z* and effective electronegativity, polarizing the O–H unit
Cl is in a lower oxidation state in HClO2, making it more electron-donating
choices.why: Cl is +1 in HClO and +3 in HClO2. Higher oxidation state means higher effective electronegativity and a more acidic E–OH.

choices.text: Oxidation lowers an atom's effective electronegativity
choices.why: When an atomic center is oxidized, its Z* and effective electronegativity increase.

choices.text: HClO2 has more hydrogen atoms to donate
choices.why: Both acids have one acidic hydrogen. The difference is the oxidation state of Cl.

explanation: When an atomic center is oxidized, its Z* and effective electronegativity increase. This shows up as greater acidity of polarized E–OH units as the central atom's oxidation state rises: HClO (Cl^{I}, pKa 7.40) < HClO2 (Cl^{III}, 1.94) < HClO3 (Cl^{V}) < HClO4 (Cl^{VII}). Electron-withdrawing substituents raise effective electronegativity in the same way.

prompt: HClO (Cl^{I}) has pKa 7.40 and HClO2 (Cl^{III}) has pKa 1.94. By what factor is the Ka of HClO2 larger than the Ka of HClO?
explanation: Ka = 10^−pKa, so Ka(HClO2)/Ka(HClO) = 10^(7.40 − 1.94) = 10^5.46 = 2.88 × 10^5. Raising the oxidation state of Cl increases its effective electronegativity and makes the O–H more acidic.

prompt: Why is there a decrease or anomalously small increase in first ionization energy from group 15 to group 16?

choices.text: The np^4 configuration has Coulombic repulsion between paired electrons that the np^3 configuration lacks
The highest occupied orbital changes from ns to np
choices.why: That explains the dip from group 2 to group 13, not from group 15 to group 16.

choices.text: The effective nuclear charge falls from group 15 to group 16
choices.why: Z* keeps rising across the row. The dip comes from electron pairing in np^4.

choices.text: Group 16 elements have a filled valence shell
choices.why: A filled valence shell belongs to the noble gases. Group 16 has np^4, with one paired p orbital.

explanation: Ionization energy does not rise smoothly across a row. From the alkaline earth metals to the boron group the highest occupied orbital changes from a lower energy ns to a higher energy np subshell. From the pnictogens to the chalcogens, Coulombic repulsion in the np^4 configuration, absent in np^3, makes the electron easier to remove.

prompt: Which statement describes the general trends in the redox properties of the main group elements (noble gases excepted)?

choices.text: Elements become better reductants toward the lower left and better oxidants toward the upper right
Elements become better oxidants toward the lower left
choices.why: The lower left holds the alkali metals, which are strong reductants. Oxidizing power rises toward fluorine at the upper right.

choices.text: Elements become stronger oxidants on moving down a group
choices.why: Down a group, elements tend to become weaker oxidants or better reductants.

choices.text: The noble gases are the strongest oxidants
choices.why: The noble gases are inert and tend not to act as good oxidants or reductants.

explanation: Very roughly, the noble gases are inert; elements toward the left act as good reductants and those toward the right as increasingly good oxidants; and down a group elements become weaker oxidants or better reductants. These trends are only approximate, since redox behavior also depends on the stability of the products.

prompt: Among the alkali metals, E°(Li^+/Li) = −3.040 V, E°(Na^+/Na) = −2.713 V, and E°(Cs^+/Cs) = −2.923 V. Why is lithium, not cesium, the most powerful reducing agent in water?

choices.text: The Li^+ cation is highly stabilized in aqueous solution by its anomalously high hydration energy
Lithium has the lowest ionization energy of the alkali metals
choices.why: Lithium has the highest ionization energy of the group; ionization energy decreases down to Cs. Hydration of Li^+ is what makes the difference.

choices.text: Lithium is the largest alkali metal
choices.why: Lithium is the smallest. Its small cation is strongly hydrated, which stabilizes Li^+ in water.

choices.text: Cesium does not react with water
choices.why: Cesium reacts explosively with water. Its reduction potential is simply less negative than lithium's.

explanation: Reduction potentials depend on the stability of both the oxidized and reduced forms. Lithium is the most powerful reductant among the alkali metals because the Li^+ ion is especially stable in water (anomalously high hydration energy). From K^+ to Cs^+ the potentials stay roughly constant, because the falling ionization energy is compensated by other factors.

prompt: For Li^+(aq) + e^− → Li(s), E° = −3.040 V. Using ΔG° = −nFE° with F = 96,485 C/mol, what is ΔG° for this reduction, in kJ/mol?
explanation: ΔG° = −nFE° = −(1)(96,485 C/mol)(−3.040 V) = +293,314 J/mol = +293.3 kJ/mol. The large positive ΔG° means Li^+ strongly resists reduction, so Li metal is a powerful reductant.

prompt: Nitrate is thermodynamically a powerful oxidant in aqueous acid, yet it usually behaves as an inert spectator ion even when strong reductants are present. Why?

choices.text: There is a large kinetic barrier to nitrate reduction; reduction potentials show whether a reaction can occur, not whether it will
Its reduction potential is actually negative
choices.why: Nitrate's reduction is thermodynamically favorable. The obstacle is kinetic, not thermodynamic.

choices.text: Nitrate cannot accept electrons because nitrogen is already in its lowest oxidation state
choices.why: Nitrogen in nitrate is +5, its highest oxidation state, so nitrate can certainly be reduced.

choices.text: Standard potentials apply only to metals
choices.why: Standard potentials apply to any half-reaction. The issue is the slow rate of nitrate reduction.

explanation: Since ΔG° = −nFE°, reduction potentials measure thermodynamic spontaneity. They tell whether a reaction can occur, not whether it actually will under a given set of conditions; kinetics must also be considered. Nitrate reduction has a large kinetic barrier, so nitrate usually acts as a spectator ion.

prompt: In a Latimer diagram, species A is reduced to B in a 2-electron step with E° = +0.80 V, and B is reduced to C in a 1-electron step with E° = +1.40 V. Using a thermodynamic cycle (free energies add, ΔG° = −nFE°), what is E° for the overall 3-electron reduction of A to C, in V?
explanation: Free energies add but potentials do not. −3FE°(A→C) = −2F(0.80 V) − 1F(1.40 V), so E°(A→C) = (2 × 0.80 + 1 × 1.40)/3 = 3.00/3 = 1.00 V.

prompt: In the Latimer diagram X —(+0.50 V)→ Y —(+1.20 V)→ Z, each step is a one-electron reduction. Is Y stable with respect to disproportionation?

choices.text: No: the potential on Y's right (+1.20 V) is more positive than the one on its left (+0.50 V), so Y disproportionates to X and Z
Yes: both potentials are positive, so every species is stable
choices.why: Positive potentials alone don't decide it. A species is unstable when the potential on its right is more positive than the one on its left.

choices.text: Yes: a species is unstable only when the potential on its left is more positive
choices.why: That's backwards. The potential on the right being more positive makes the species unstable to disproportionation.

choices.text: It cannot be decided without knowing the pH
choices.why: The diagram already gives the potentials for its conditions; comparing them is enough.

explanation: A species is unstable with respect to disproportionation if the potential on its right is more positive than that on its left. Here the reduction Y → Z (+1.20 V) is more favorable than the reduction X → Y (+0.50 V), so 2Y → X + Z has E° = 1.20 − 0.50 = +0.70 V and is favored.

prompt: In a Latimer diagram, the one-electron reduction of M^4+ to M^3+ has E° = +1.85 V, and the one-electron reduction of M^5+ to M^4+ has E° = +0.95 V. What is E° for the disproportionation 2M^4+ → M^5+ + M^3+, in V?
explanation: Split it into halves. Reduction: M^4+ + e^− → M^3+, E° = +1.85 V. Oxidation: M^4+ → M^5+ + e^−, E° = −0.95 V. Both steps transfer one electron, so the potentials add directly: E° = 1.85 − 0.95 = +0.90 V. The positive value means M^4+ is unstable to disproportionation.

prompt: In a Frost diagram, NE° is plotted against oxidation state N. What does a negative NE° value for an oxidation state indicate?

choices.text: That state is more stable than the free element
That state is less stable than the free element
choices.why: NE° is proportional to free energy relative to the element. Negative values mean the state is lower in free energy, so more stable.

choices.text: That state is a negative oxidation state
choices.why: The sign of NE° is not the sign of the oxidation state; positive oxidation states can have negative NE° (like Ni^2+).

choices.text: That state cannot exist in water
choices.why: A negative NE° indicates a state more stable than the element; nickel's Ni^2+ is an example in acid.

explanation: NE° is proportional to the standard free energy for converting the free element to that oxidation state, so the lower its value, the more stable the state. Negative values mean the state is more stable than the element; positive values mean it is less stable. For example, Ni^2+ lies below Ni, so nickel dissolves in nonoxidizing acid, while Cu^+ and Cu^2+ lie above Cu.

prompt: For a metal M in acid, E°(M^2+/M) = −0.40 V (2 electrons) and E°(M^3+/M^2+) = +0.60 V (1 electron). What is NE°, in V, for the +3 oxidation state on M's Frost diagram?
explanation: NE° for a state is the sum of n × E° for the steps linking it to the element. For +2: NE° = 2 × (−0.40 V) = −0.80 V. For +3: NE° = −0.80 V + 1 × (+0.60 V) = −0.20 V.

prompt: On a Frost diagram, a tie-line is drawn between two oxidation states. What does it mean if an intermediate state lies above that line?

choices.text: The intermediate state is unstable toward disproportionation to the two states at the ends of the line
The intermediate state will form by comproportionation of the two end states
choices.why: States lying below a tie-line are the ones formed by comproportionation; a state above the line disproportionates.

choices.text: The intermediate state is the most stable state of the element
choices.why: The most stable state is the lowest point on the diagram. A point above a tie-line is unstable toward disproportionation.

choices.text: Nothing: only adjacent states can be compared
choices.why: Tie-lines between nonadjacent states are exactly how the systematic analysis is done.

explanation: The slope of a line between two points on a Frost diagram equals the standard potential interconverting them. A state above a tie-line is unstable toward disproportionation to the states at its ends, because the reduction half-reaction then has a more positive potential than the oxidation. Conversely, if a state lies below the line between two species, those two species can comproportionate to form it.

prompt: On a Pourbaix diagram, what kind of equilibrium gives a vertical line?

choices.text: An acid–base equilibrium with no change in oxidation state, such as 2Fe^3+ + 3H2O → Fe2O3(s) + 6H^+
An electron-transfer equilibrium with no H^+ involved, such as Fe^3+ + e^− → Fe^2+
choices.why: Its potential doesn't depend on pH, so it gives a horizontal line.

choices.text: An equilibrium that involves both electron transfer and H^+, such as Fe2O3 + 6H^+ + 2e^− → 2Fe^2+ + 3H2O
choices.why: Combined electron-transfer and acid–base equilibria give slanted lines, since the potential depends on pH.

choices.text: The reduction of water to H2
choices.why: Water reduction involves both H^+ and electrons, so its line slopes with pH.

explanation: Electron transfer alone gives horizontal lines (the potential doesn't depend on pH). Acid–base equilibria with no redox change give vertical lines, at a pH set by the concentration used to draw the diagram. Equilibria involving both electron transfer and H^+ give slanted lines.

prompt: Metallic iron is not thermodynamically stable in oxygen-containing water, yet an oxide coating can protect it from further oxidation. What kind of stabilization is this?

choices.text: Kinetic stabilization (anodic passivation): the solid oxide layer insulates the iron from reaction with oxygen
Thermodynamic stabilization: the oxide coating makes metallic iron the most stable species
choices.why: Iron remains thermodynamically unstable at the potential set by O2. The coating only slows the reaction.

choices.text: Cathodic protection by a more reactive metal
choices.why: Cathodic protection couples the metal to a more reactive metal that oxidizes instead. Passivation relies on the metal's own oxide layer.

choices.text: Raising the potential above the oxygen line
choices.why: Passivation doesn't change the potential; a solid oxide layer physically blocks further reaction.

explanation: The O2 reduction potential lies above the stability region of metallic iron, so Fe is not thermodynamically stable under these conditions. At higher pH, oxidation gives solid oxides. If they coat the surface and insulate the metal from oxygen, they prevent further oxidation. Such layers are passivating, and anodic passivation is a kinetic, not thermodynamic, stabilization.
